title: Aldehydes and Ketones
description: The carbonyl group and its nucleophilic addition reactions: hydrates, acetals, imines, cyanohydrins, Wittig alkenes and reductions.
overview: The carbonyl group, C=O, is the most important functional group in organic chemistry. It appears in sugars, fats, proteins, drugs and nearly every synthetic target, and its reactions form carbon–carbon bonds and interconvert most other functional groups. The key to all of it is one idea: the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, and nucleophiles attack it.
This chapter covers the structure and reactivity of aldehydes and ketones and the nucleophilic addition reactions that follow: water, alcohols, cyanide, amines, phosphorus ylides and hydrides.
objectives: Name aldehydes and ketones and explain their electrophilic reactivity.
Write mechanisms for nucleophilic addition under basic and acidic conditions.
Predict the equilibrium of hydrate and hemiacetal formation, and use acetals as protecting groups.
Form imines, enamines and oximes, and carry out reductive amination.
Plan alkene syntheses with the Wittig and Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reactions.
Choose reagents to reduce a carbonyl to an alcohol or a methylene, and to oxidize aldehydes.

sections.title: The carbonyl group
body: In a carbonyl group the carbon is sp² and trigonal planar, with bond angles near 120°. The C=O bond is strongly polar because oxygen is much more electronegative: the carbon carries partial positive charge, and the oxygen partial negative. In resonance terms, the zwitterionic contributor C⁺–O⁻ contributes significantly. The carbon is therefore an **electrophile**, attacked by nucleophiles from either face along a path at about 107° to the C=O bond (the Bürgi–Dunitz angle), and the oxygen is weakly basic (the pK_a of a protonated ketone is about −7).

An **aldehyde** has at least one H on the carbonyl carbon (RCHO, named -al, such as ethanal, CH₃CHO), and a **ketone** has two carbons (RCOR′, named -one: propanone, or acetone). The carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde is numbered C1. In IR spectra the C=O stretch is a strong, sharp band near 1715 cm⁻¹ for ketones and 1730 cm⁻¹ for aldehydes (which also show C–H stretches near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹).

Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones, for two reasons. Sterically, an H is smaller than an alkyl group, so the nucleophile approaches more easily and the product is less crowded. Electronically, the alkyl groups of a ketone donate electron density to the carbonyl carbon and stabilize it, which reduces its electrophilicity. Formaldehyde is the most reactive and benzaldehyde, whose carbonyl is conjugated with the ring, is less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes.

sections.title: Nucleophilic addition: mechanism and equilibria
body: The fundamental reaction of aldehydes and ketones is **nucleophilic addition**. The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the C=O π electrons move to oxygen to give a tetrahedral alkoxide, and protonation gives the neutral product. The carbon changes from sp² to sp³.

list: **Strong nucleophiles** (hydride, Grignard reagents, acetylide, cyanide) add irreversibly, because the product alkoxide is a poor leaving group. The attack is the rate-determining step, and the protonation is a separate workup step.

**Weak nucleophiles** (water, alcohols, amines) need help. Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen first, making the carbon a far better electrophile (activation by acid). Base catalysis works through a more nucleophilic anion. These additions are reversible, and the position of equilibrium matters.

body: Water adds to give a **hydrate** (geminal diol): R₂C=O + H₂O ⇌ R₂C(OH)₂. Equilibrium favors the hydrate only for the most electrophilic carbonyls. Formaldehyde in water is more than 99.9% hydrate (K = 2 × 10³), acetaldehyde about 58% (K = 1.0), and acetone only 0.14% (K = 1.4 × 10⁻³). Electron-withdrawing groups favor hydrates: chloral (CCl₃CHO) and ninhydrin form stable crystalline hydrates. The hydrate is why oxidation of an aldehyde under aqueous conditions goes through to the acid.

Hydrogen cyanide (made in situ from NaCN and acid, since HCN is gaseous and highly toxic) adds to give a **cyanohydrin**, R₂C(OH)C≡N. It adds one carbon to the skeleton, and the nitrile can be hydrolyzed to an α-hydroxy acid (with H₃O⁺, heat) or reduced to a β-amino alcohol (LiAlH₄). The reaction is reversible and favorable for aldehydes and unhindered ketones.

example.title: Chain extension
example.solution: Add NaCN and acid to benzaldehyde to give mandelonitrile, PhCH(OH)CN. Hydrolyze the nitrile with aqueous acid and heat to the acid: mandelic acid, with one more carbon than the starting material.

sections.title: Hemiacetals and acetals
body: An alcohol adds to a carbonyl to give a **hemiacetal** (R₂C(OH)OR′), usually unfavorable for simple ketones, but easy for aldehydes and favorable intramolecularly: a hydroxy aldehyde with the OH four or five carbons away cyclizes to a five- or six-membered cyclic hemiacetal. This is how sugars exist in solution (glucose is more than 99% cyclic).

With acid catalysis and a second equivalent of alcohol, the hemiacetal is protonated, loses water to give an oxocarbenium ion, and a second alcohol adds to give an **acetal** (R₂C(OR′)₂). Each step is reversible. To make the acetal, remove the water (a Dean–Stark trap, or excess alcohol with a dehydrating agent), and to hydrolyze it, add excess aqueous acid. Using ethylene glycol gives a five-membered **cyclic acetal** (a 1,3-dioxolane), which is favored entropically.

body.key: Acetals are stable to base, to nucleophiles, to Grignard reagents and to hydrides, but are hydrolyzed by aqueous acid. This makes them ideal protecting groups for aldehydes and ketones.

example.title: Selective reduction using an acetal
example.problem: Reduce only the ester in methyl 4-oxopentanoate (CH₃COCH₂CH₂COOCH₃) to give 5-hydroxypentan-2-one.
solution: LiAlH₄ would reduce both the ketone and the ester, and NaBH₄ would reduce the ketone but not the ester, giving the wrong product.

Protect the ketone as its cyclic acetal (ethylene glycol, H⁺, remove water). Reduce the ester with LiAlH₄ to the primary alcohol (the acetal is inert to hydride). Remove the protecting group with H₃O⁺, which regenerates the ketone.

sections.title: Reactions with nitrogen nucleophiles
body: A primary amine adds to the carbonyl, and after proton transfers loses water to give an **imine** (Schiff base, R₂C=N–R′). A secondary amine, which has no second N–H to lose, gives an **enamine** (C=C–N), losing a proton from the α carbon instead. Both reactions are acid-catalyzed and reversible, and the rate peaks near pH 4.5: below that the amine is protonated and not nucleophilic, and above it there is too little acid to activate the carbonyl and to protonate the OH of the carbinolamine so that water can leave.

body: An imine can be reduced as it forms. Treating a carbonyl compound and an amine with NaBH₃CN (sodium cyanoborohydride) or NaBH(OAc)₃ at about pH 6 gives an amine in one pot. The reagent is mild enough that it does not reduce the carbonyl, but reduces the iminium ion. This is the most useful way to make secondary and tertiary amines, since direct alkylation of amines overreacts.

To convert C=O to CH₂, use the **Wolff–Kishner** reduction (hydrazine, KOH, ethylene glycol, 200 °C: basic conditions, through the hydrazone and loss of N₂) or the **Clemmensen** reduction (zinc amalgam, concentrated HCl: acidic conditions). Choose according to which the rest of the molecule tolerates. Together with Friedel–Crafts acylation they give straight-chain alkylbenzenes.

example.title: Reductive amination
example.solution: Mix cyclohexanone and methylamine with NaBH₃CN at pH about 6. The imine forms in equilibrium and is reduced to the secondary amine.

sections.title: The Wittig reaction
body: The **Wittig reaction** converts a C=O into a C=C with predictable placement of the double bond: R₂C=O + Ph₃P=CHR′ → R₂C=CHR′ + Ph₃P=O. The reagent is a phosphorus **ylide** (a neutral species with adjacent opposite charges, ⁻CHR′–PPh₃⁺). It is made in two steps: SN2 of triphenylphosphine on a primary alkyl halide gives a phosphonium salt, and a strong base (n-BuLi, NaH) removes the acidic α-proton (pK_a about 22).

The ylide carbon attacks the carbonyl to give a betaine or directly a four-membered **oxaphosphetane**, which collapses to the alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide. The strong P=O bond (about 540 kJ mol⁻¹) drives the reaction. The double bond forms exactly where the C=O was, with no mixture of positional isomers, unlike elimination reactions.

list: **Stabilized ylides** (R′ = C=O, CN: Ph₃P=CHCO₂Et) are less reactive and give mainly **E**-alkenes.

The **Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons (HWE)** reaction uses a phosphonate carbanion, (EtO)₂P(O)CH⁻CO₂Et, with an aldehyde or ketone. It gives E-α,β-unsaturated esters with high selectivity, the by-product (a water-soluble phosphate) is easily removed, and the reagents react with hindered ketones that stabilized Wittig ylides do not.

example.title: Methylenation
example.solution: Prepare Ph₃P=CH₂ from CH₃Br: Ph₃P + CH₃Br gives Ph₃P⁺CH₃ Br⁻, then n-BuLi. Add cyclohexanone: the oxaphosphetane collapses to methylenecyclohexane and Ph₃P=O. Acid-catalyzed elimination from 1-methylcyclohexanol would give the more substituted 1-methylcyclohexene instead; the Wittig reaction gives the exocyclic alkene specifically.

check.a: Formation of the strong P=O bond in triphenylphosphine oxide
wrong: Formation of a C–C σ bond only

sections.title: Reduction and oxidation of carbonyl compounds
body: Hydride donors reduce carbonyls to alcohols by nucleophilic addition of H⁻ followed by protonation. **Sodium borohydride** (NaBH₄, in ethanol or methanol) reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters, acids or amides, and tolerates water and alcohols. **Lithium aluminum hydride** (LiAlH₄, in ether) is far more reactive and reduces nearly all carbonyls, including acids and esters (to primary alcohols) and amides (to amines), and reacts violently with water. Both attack with equal facility from the less hindered face of a cyclic ketone: small hydrides prefer axial attack (giving the equatorial alcohol), and bulky hydrides (L-Selectride) attack equatorially.

**Aldehydes oxidize easily** because of their aldehyde hydrogen, to carboxylic acids, with any oxidant from Jones reagent to air. Ketones resist oxidation without breaking C–C bonds. The ease distinguishes the two classes. In **Tollens’ test** an aldehyde reduces the silver–ammonia complex, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, to metallic silver, which plates the test tube as a mirror, while ketones do not react. **Fehling’s** and Benedict’s tests use Cu(II), which gives a red Cu₂O precipitate with aliphatic aldehydes. These tests also identify reducing sugars.

An aldehyde with no α-hydrogens, such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde, on treatment with concentrated hydroxide undergoes the **Cannizzaro reaction**, a disproportionation: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidized to the carboxylate, 2 PhCHO + OH⁻ → PhCH₂OH + PhCOO⁻.

quiz.q: Benzaldehyde is less reactive toward nucleophiles than butanal. The reason is that
quiz.a: conjugation with the ring donates electron density to the carbonyl carbon
wrong: the flat ring blocks the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon
the ring withdraws electron density from the carbonyl carbon by induction
benzaldehyde has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, unlike aliphatic aldehydes
quiz.why: Resonance with the ring spreads positive character away from the carbonyl carbon, lowering its electrophilicity. Benzaldehyde does have the aldehyde H, and the ring is no more hindering than a small alkyl group.

quiz.q: A compound has a strong IR band at 1730 cm⁻¹ and weak bands at 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹. It is most likely
quiz.why: The pair of C–H stretches near 2720 and 2820 cm⁻¹ belongs to the aldehyde hydrogen. A ketone has the C=O band but not these, and alcohols and ethers lack a carbonyl band.

quiz.q: Why is the addition of a Grignard reagent to a ketone irreversible, whereas hydrate formation is reversible?
quiz.a: R⁻ is a very poor leaving group, so the alkoxide cannot revert, whereas a hydrate readily loses water or hydroxide
wrong: Grignard additions release a gas, which removes the product from the equilibrium as it forms, unlike hydrations
Hydrate formation changes the carbon from sp² to sp³, but Grignard addition leaves it trigonal planar
The Grignard product is stabilized by hydrogen bonding to the ether solvent, which prevents reversal
quiz.why: Reversal needs a leaving group. R⁻ from a Grignard is a very poor one, whereas a hydrate can lose water or hydroxide and return to the carbonyl.

quiz.q: A carbonyl compound hydrates with equilibrium constant K = [hydrate]/[carbonyl] = 9. What percentage is present as the hydrate?
quiz.why: The hydrate fraction is K/(1 + K) = 9/10. Reading K as a percentage gives 9%, and 10% is the fraction of carbonyl that remains.

quiz.q: Chloral (CCl₃CHO) forms a stable, crystalline hydrate. This is because the CCl₃ group
quiz.a: withdraws electrons, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and less stabilized
wrong: donates electrons to the carbonyl carbon, which stabilizes the resulting diol by resonance
hydrogen-bonds to incoming water, holding it close to the carbonyl carbon
blocks every other addition reaction, so hydration is the only path left
quiz.why: Electron-withdrawing groups destabilize the C=O relative to the sp³ hydrate, so the equilibrium shifts toward the gem-diol.

quiz.q: A cyanohydrin R₂C(OH)C≡N is treated with LiAlH₄ and then water. The product is
quiz.why: LiAlH₄ reduces the nitrile C≡N to CH₂NH₂. The α-hydroxy acid is what hydrolysis with H₃O⁺ and heat would give.

wrong: a five-membered cyclic acetal, with a second OR group
quiz.why: The OH adds to the carbonyl carbon intramolecularly, giving a ring of the four carbons and the oxygen. It has only one OR group and one OH on the former carbonyl carbon, so it is a hemiacetal.

quiz.q: To make a Grignard reagent from 4-bromobutanal, the aldehyde is first converted to an acetal. Why?
quiz.a: The Grignard reagent would add to the C=O of another molecule, but acetals are inert to it
wrong: Magnesium metal would reduce the aldehyde to an alcohol before the Grignard reagent could form
Acetal formation makes the C–Br bond more reactive toward insertion of magnesium metal
Acetals are the only functional groups that dissolve in the ether solvent
quiz.why: A Grignard reagent attacks carbonyls. An acetal is stable to bases and nucleophiles, so the reagent can be made and used, and aqueous acid later restores the aldehyde.

quiz.q: A secondary amine adds to a ketone, and the intermediate loses water. Why does the product end up as an enamine and not a neutral imine?
quiz.a: The nitrogen has no second N–H to lose, so an α hydrogen is lost instead
wrong: Secondary amines cannot add to the carbonyl carbon
The carbinolamine from a secondary amine cannot lose water under any conditions
The C=N bond of an imine is always hydrolyzed under the reaction conditions
quiz.why: Loss of water gives an iminium ion. With no N–H to remove, the base takes an α hydrogen to give C=C–N. A primary amine can lose its N–H and stop at the imine.

quiz.q: Reductive amination is run with NaBH₃CN rather than NaBH₄ at pH about 6 because NaBH₃CN
quiz.a: reduces the iminium ion far faster than the ketone, so the ketone lasts long enough to form the imine
wrong: is a stronger hydride donor, so it reduces the carbonyl and the iminium ion at similar rates
cannot reduce any C=N bond, which prevents the amine product from being reduced further
reacts with the amine to make the iminium ion, so no acid catalyst is needed
quiz.why: The reagent is selective for the protonated C=N⁺ over C=O. The amine product forms in one pot instead of the alcohol that a stronger hydride would give.

quiz.q: Butan-2-one and dimethylamine are treated with NaBH₃CN at pH about 6. The product is
quiz.why: The secondary amine forms an iminium ion at the carbonyl carbon, and hydride adds there. The nitrogen ends up on C2 with two methyl groups, so the product is a tertiary amine.

quiz.q: A ketone also contains a cyclic acetal that must be kept. Which method converts C=O to CH₂?
quiz.why: Wolff–Kishner is basic, and acetals survive base. Clemmensen uses concentrated HCl, which would hydrolyze the acetal.

quiz.q: How is the ylide Ph₃P=CHCH₃ made?
quiz.a: Ph₃P is alkylated with CH₃CH₂Br, then the phosphonium salt is deprotonated with n-BuLi
wrong: it gives Z-α,β-unsaturated esters selectively, which a stabilized ylide never does
it produces triphenylphosphine oxide, which crystallizes and is therefore easily removed
it works only with unstabilized ylides, so it avoids ester groups
quiz.why: SN2 of triphenylphosphine on a primary halide gives the phosphonium salt, whose α-H (pK_a about 22) needs a strong base. A weak base such as bicarbonate is not strong enough.

quiz.q: Which combination gives (E)-ethyl cinnamate, PhCH=CHCO₂Et, with high E selectivity?
wrong: benzyl alcohol, PhCH₂OH, as esters and acids would give
benzaldehyde, PhCHO, after hydrolysis of an intermediate imine
quiz.why: The ester-stabilized ylide adds to benzaldehyde to place the new double bond between the two carbons, and stabilized ylides give mainly the E alkene.

quiz.q: An organic chemist prefers a Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reagent to a stabilized Wittig ylide for a hindered ketone mainly because
quiz.a: the phosphonate carbanion is more reactive, and its phosphate by-product is water-soluble
wrong: it gives Z alkenes selectively, which Wittig ylides cannot
it produces triphenylphosphine oxide, which is easy to crystallize
it works only with unstabilized ylides, so it avoids ester groups
quiz.why: Phosphonate carbanions add to ketones that stabilized ylides ignore, and the phosphate is washed out with water. They also give E-α,β-unsaturated esters.

quiz.q: Benzamide, PhCONH₂, is treated with excess LiAlH₄, and then water is added. The product is
quiz.why: LiAlH₄ reduces amides to amines, in contrast to esters and acids, which give alcohols. NaBH₄ would leave the amide alone.

quiz.q: Which pair of compounds can be distinguished by Tollens’ reagent?
quiz.why: Only the aldehyde is oxidized and reduces [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ to a silver mirror. Each other pair gives no reaction in either member.

quiz.q: Which compound undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction in concentrated NaOH?
quiz.why: Cannizzaro needs an aldehyde with no α-hydrogens, so that it cannot form an enolate. Aldehydes with α-H, such as propanal and phenylacetaldehyde, react at the α carbon instead.

summary: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones, because of less steric hindrance and less electron donation.
Strong nucleophiles add irreversibly. Weak ones add reversibly and need acid activation. Hydrate formation depends on carbonyl electrophilicity.
Acetals protect carbonyls from base and nucleophiles and are removed with aqueous acid.
Primary amines give imines and secondary amines give enamines, with optimum pH near 4.5. Reductive amination makes amines. Wolff–Kishner and Clemmensen convert C=O to CH₂.
The Wittig reaction makes C=C exactly where C=O was. Unstabilized ylides give Z, and stabilized ylides and HWE give E.
NaBH₄ reduces aldehydes and ketones. LiAlH₄ reduces all carbonyls. Aldehydes (not ketones) are oxidized easily, as in Tollens’ test.

problems.q: Predict the products: (a) cyclopentanone + NaBH₄, then H₃O⁺; (b) acetophenone + CH₃NH₂, H⁺, then NaBH₃CN; (c) butanal + Ph₃P=CHCH₃; (d) acetone + ethylene glycol, H⁺, with water removed.
problems.solution: (a) Cyclopentanol. (b) N-Methyl-1-phenylethylamine. (c) Hex-2-ene, mainly (Z). (d) The cyclic acetal 2,2-dimethyl-1,3-dioxolane.

problems.q: Outline the synthesis of 1-phenylpropene (PhCH=CHCH₃) by two Wittig routes.
problems.solution: (1) Benzaldehyde + the ylide from ethyl bromide (Ph₃P=CHCH₃). (2) Acetaldehyde + the ylide from benzyl bromide (Ph₃P=CHPh, which is stabilized by the phenyl and favors E).

problems.q: Explain why the rate of imine formation is highest near pH 4.5 and falls at lower and higher pH.
problems.solution: The first step needs a free amine as nucleophile, which is protonated and unreactive at low pH. The loss of water from the carbinolamine needs acid to protonate the OH. At high pH there is too little acid for this step, which becomes rate-limiting.
problems.a: A compromise between a free amine at high pH and acid catalysis at low pH.

problems.q: Convert cyclohexanone into 1-hydroxycyclohexanecarboxylic acid, adding one carbon.
problems.solution: Add NaCN with acid to cyclohexanone to form the cyanohydrin, 1-hydroxycyclohexanecarbonitrile. Hydrolyze the nitrile with aqueous acid and heat to give 1-hydroxycyclohexanecarboxylic acid.
